newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani bankers say borrowing target ambitious.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani bankers say borrowing target ambitious.

text.p: Government borrowing targets set by Pakistan's central bank for fiscal 1997/98 will be difficult to meet, bankers said on Thursday.
"The borrowing target for the government is very ambitious," Mohammad Umer, treasury analyst at Banque Indosuez, told Reuters.

The State (central) Bank of Pakistan on Wednesday fixed total government borrowing for budgetary support in fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) at 58 billion rupees ($1.43 billion) and monetary expansion at 14 percent.

Government borrowing for 1996/97 was likely to reach a record 120 billion rupees against an original target of 20 billion and revised target of 44 billion rupees, said a treasury head of a foreign bank, who asked not be named.

"Even if the government resorts to window-dressing by forcing state-run banks to borrow back part of the amount they lend it will be very difficult to bring the final figure below 100 billion rupees," said the banker.

He added high borrowing by Pakistan for budgetary support may cause difficulties with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which is monitoring Pakistan's macroeconomy before starting negotiations on a new, medium-term loan.
The IMF and Pakistan officials are expected to discuss an enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) in July after Pakistan presents its budget in June.

The central bank on Wednesday also approved credit requirements of the private sector at 82 billion rupees for 1997/98. It also lowered the statutory liquidity reserve (SLR) which banks are required to maintain by five percentage points to 20 percent of total deposits.
Bankers said the cut in the SLR would inject about 45 billion rupees into the market and may help bring down lending rates for the corporate sector in the next fiscal year.
The immediate beneficiary of the move would be the government itself as most banks have already utilised their limits set in the corporate sector credit plan for 1996/97, they said.
"The market was already very liquid," Umer said, and added that setting free more money by cutting the SLR would mean lower yields on the government's six-month bonds.

The State Bank of Pakistan on Wednesday auctioned six-month federal bonds worth a total of 1.8 billion rupees in its weekly open market operations at a maximum yield of 16.95 percent, compared to 17.50 percent at the previous auction.

"It seems the government will be able to keep bond yields down for the the next three to six months," Umer said. He added that lending rates for the corporate sector would only fall if the government kept within its borrowing target.
Bankers said private companies were borrowing at an average of 22 to 23 percent a year, but the cut in SLR could bring the rate down to 19 to 20 percent.
